H5N1 in US dairy cattle and poultry, 2025
Poultry
Winter wave: The February egg price spike followed the culling of 41.4 million infected or exposed birds in December 2024 and January 2025. That was the most lethal two-month period of the outbreak.[1]
Cumulative toll: Since the virus re-emerged in February 2022, the US outbreak has caused the confirmed loss of over 175 million birds across 1,700+ flocks.[2] Table-egg-laying hens were the most affected, accounting for 75% of domestic poultry loss.[3]
Egg prices: The national average retail price hit an all-time high of $6.23 per dozen in March 2025.[3] It fell to $5.12 in April and $4.55 in May as wholesale prices dropped.[3] Between May 2024 and April 2025, one analysis estimated Americans spent an extra $14.5 billion on eggs.[4]
Response: In February 2025, the Trump administration announced a $1 billion plan to fight the virus and bring down egg prices.[5]
Later in the year: One analysis noted that egg prices were showing signs of bottoming out or rising slightly again as bird flu rebounded.[6]
Dairy cattle
Herds affected: Between March 2024 and 1 July 2025, 1,074 dairy herds in 17 states tested positive.[7] Most of those herds were infected in 2024.
New spillovers: Until early 2025, all detections in cattle were genotype B3.13. A second genotype, D1.1, was then confirmed in dairy cattle in Nevada and Arizona.[8] These were two additional, separate bird-to-cow spillover events.[7]
Slowdown: Detections in dairy herds dropped significantly after April 2025, despite a surge in Idaho that month.[7] Researchers also saw a notable decrease in interstate spread, helped by control measures.[9]
Severity: Mortality in infected cattle is only about 2%, but reduced and abnormal milk production can still have serious financial impacts.[1] Dairy prices have been relatively insulated from HPAI, unlike eggs.[1]
Vaccines: No vaccination programs had been approved in the US for dairy cattle.[9]
Human and other effects
70 human H5 cases had been reported in the US since April 2024[10] as of March 2025. Another source reports no new human cases after March 2025.[9]
Over 70 H5 infections were confirmed in domestic cats in the US in 2025.[7]
If you want more on one piece, such as vaccine policy, milk testing, or the fall 2025 poultry resurgence, I can look into it.
